newsitem.title: USA: Motorola launches smartcard business unit.
newsitem.headline: Motorola launches smartcard business unit.

text.p: Technology giant Motorola Inc is launching a new business unit to enter the smartcard market, which could eventually let users personalize their smartcards to pay for their daily train commute or groceries at the supermarket, the company said Thursday.

Smartcards look like credit cards but have an embedded microprocessor that gives them capabilities of a minicomputer. According to Motorola, a report by industry analyst group Dataquest predicted the market for microprocessor-based smartcards would grow to 1.2 billion units in 2001 from 84 million in 1995.
Motorola said it expects it will ship the unit's first products by the end of the year. Initial markets include transportation and banking.
The new unit, Smartcard Systems Business, will be part of Motorola's Land Mobile Products Sector in Schaumburg. The new business will be headed by Mark Davies, vice president of the smartcard unit.
Smartcard Systems Business will provide a range of products for smartcards, including the cards, readers and software needed to use them.

"Key to success for the new unit will be Motorola's ability to leverage its core competence in radio frequency systems and software, together with its role as the world's leading provider of microprocessors for smartcards," the company said.

Motorola said the business unit will actively pursue partnerships and alliances with other companies. The unit will be independent of the company's Semiconductor Products Sector, which already supplies chips to the smartcard market.
"As in the personal computer industry, enhancements in semiconductors and software will drive consumer adoption of smartcards," Davies said in a statement.

"Ultimately, we believe consumers will personalize their individual smartcards, selecting applications such as electronic commerce and frequent-user programs that are important in enhancing personal and business life," he said.

Smartcards have been used for two decades but are becoming increasingly complex. Initially they were used as debit cards for a French bank and required insertion of the card into a terminal to transmit information. They are also used as telephone cards.
The new cards have computing power comparable to early personal computers. Some cards use radio technology to send and receive information without coming into physical contact with a terminal.
Motorola said combination cards, providing "both contacted and contactless methods" of transferring information, are the next generation.
Motorola provides wireless communications, semiconductors, and advanced electronic systems, components and services.
